The “it would be lovely but we can’t afford it” excuse regarding universal healthcare is just a cop-out. The virus Phi X-174 (by the way, the "X" is the Roman numeral 10) has a long history in genomics because of its small genome size. Frederick Sanger and colleagues at the MRC in Cambridge England developed an ingenious but difficult method for sequencing DNA and in a tour de force publication in the journal Nature in 1977 presented its complete genome sequence (~5000 bases) .  A few weeks after it was published, I saw Sanger give a talk on it, and it was the closest to a standing ovation I've ever seen for a scientific talk. We knew a revolution in biology had begun. 
Sanger had already won a Nobel Prize in 1958 for developing methods for sequencing proteins, and won another in 1980 for DNA sequencing. Eventually Sanger's group made improvements in the sequencing methodology and the first bacterial genome sequence (ca. 1.8 million base pairs) was published in 1995. Eventually automated sequencing machines were developed and improved and a draft human genome sequence (ca. 3 billion base pairs) was published in 2000. Now any lab can obtain billions of bases of raw DNA sequence; however, it all started with PhiX174.

This is a good piece. But let me just say that if you are on anti-depressants and they help you, you have nothing to be ashamed about or obligation to stop taking them. The idea of "natural" living in this intensely unnatural world is not something you have to chain yourself to. Take care of yourself.

I have had severe mental health problems in my life, that go beyond depression, and they are well-controlled - but only because of medication. Although medicine and pharma likely overstated the benefits of anti-depressants over the last few decades, for some people, psychiatric drugs are borderline necessary.

At the same time, many people could benefit from going off the drugs. As much as I have drugs that have helped me, I have had drugs that it was important I stop taking, because they weren't right for me. But if an SSRI/NSAID user hasn't improved the conditions in their life that led to the depression in the first place, it will likely return.

comments.body:
I was always a nervous kid. My parents had to install silent light switches when I was a baby, or I'd wake up and cry. Over the years, a mix of self-regulation and, uh, self-medication got me through high school and college. 

Hitting the workforce was like a brick wall. The stresses and structures of an office were brutal. The depression and anxiety grew to where I was going to lose my job and my relationship. I could have gone to a dark place. So I saw a psychiatrist, and started on SSRIs. I've been on them for 23 years. 

I've tried to stop, but the withdrawal is real. It's hard to do that *and* have a life. And my life is good, despite some lingering depression and anxiety. Good marriage, kids, decent job, fun and adventure. But I wonder if I still need SSRIs, or what I'm missing, or if I could do better. Next, I'm trying transcranial magnetic stimulation and talk therapy. Then I'll see if I can reduce or taper off the pills. As it is, I'm lucky not to be worse off.

Looking back, maybe if I was a farmer, or a monk, or filthy rich and doing whatever I wanted, I wouldn't need these things. But I'm not, and the world isn't built for people with natures like mine. Maybe it never was and people just suffered.

If an SSRI gets you through this life, take it. There are worse fates. Or try other things. There's no one answer, and lots of opinions. Just know that there's all kinds of help, and more than one way to feel better. We're fortunate to have so many choices.

The only time I suffered depression since starting meds was when I tapered off them, and the result was the worst, and nearly fatal, depression of my life. I’m grateful for this drug (at the same time,  I am also aware that we live in an era where psycho-pharmaceuticals are over-prescribed, and the social/industrial etiology of psychological disorders is poorly understood).

I understand truly contextualizing this bit below would, perhaps, be unwieldy, but there is so much room left in the vagueness here: 

“ Studies suggest that over the past few decades, affective polarization in the United States has grown faster than ideological polarization…”

How significant is the current divide between the affective polarization and the ideological polarization of Americans? That really matters here, right? If affective polarization only marginally outpaces ideological polarization, then the conclusion drawn here is kind of moot. 

Additionally, the author claims that affective polarization is “when your politics become a core feature of your identity, leading you to have negative feelings toward those that disagree with you,” as if your identity and foundational morals do not inform or, at the very least, impact your politics. As other commenters are referencing in their anecdotes, opting against a university within a state that disallows abortion or opting for a university that considers LGBTQ identities valid do not feel like the dangerous results of silly affective polarization but instead feels like genuinely pragmatic decision making. And this is because politics *do* matter and there is an obvious and real ideological rift. 

I suspect the author believes these types of examples are exceptions, but this is why I think the article does need more context regarding how and how significantly affective polarization has outpaced ideological polarization.

In the mid-1990s I picked a college in large part because of its politics and take on social issues. At freshmen orientation there was a set of skits called "PC" skits that was making fun of the fact that the school and student body were what today would be considered "woke".  There were some conservatives on campus, but they were few and far between and they were not loud.  I studied politics, and the liberal leaning of the school didn't stop us from studying and discussing various view points.  

My wife on the other hand went to one of the premiere private Christian schools in the country.  She picked it because of its conservative Christian values and stances.  Professors and students had to sign confessional statements and codes of conduct that were explicitly political.  Unlike my more liberal school, what teachers and students could say and discuss was formally bounded.  Those limits later pushed her in a more liberal direction, but liberal politics were rare. 

I've worked with college students on social justice issues in various capacities for much of the last twenty years, and these same divides have always been present.  

The political subdivisions in schools and people grouping together isn't so new.  What is new is the political obsession with these divisions and the push by conservatives to legislate their views into schools where they otherwise would not fit.

Complaining about the degree of polarization reads to me as a lazy attempt to weigh in without saying anything material about the factors that divide people. You're not going to stop an argument by covering your ears and saying "please stop fighting!"

The reality is that the cultural factors at play here do not originate with college experiences, and are expressed across the associative choices of a much broader range of people than college students. Making the ship change course will require monumental efforts towards a political realignment that is against the interests of just about every person who wields significant political, economic, or media power in the country.

They go to houses of worship that align with their political beliefs. I would argue that colleges and universities, as imperfect as they may be, still expose students to more diversity of thought (or at least the option of diversity of thought if the right courses are chosen) than other institutions. The Rhine River has never been all that easy a river to navigate without some adjustments.    At only a bit under 800 miles in its full corrected length, it has been subject to major difficulties to make it relatively easily traveled. 

The Rhine still requires at least a lock system as used in the panama canal to create the more easy travel along the river.    From 1817 a large reengineering project had to be started to remove a hairpin curve from the river which was not at all likely to see good passage possible, this being the Tulla Project.   Beyond that, the River had areas of rather limited depth which had to be dredged out and many areas saw the need to remove river bed deposits of large boulders which created a hazard for commercial craft travel. 
Much of this is to be found described in detail in MarK Cioc's work, The Rhine: an Eco-Biography 1815-2000, Seattle: U. Washington Press c. 2002 
The river is a major commercial and tourist artery for at least 5 Nations [Switzerland, France, Germany, Belgium and the Netherlands].
It is clearly now under threat!

comments.name: Devout Skeptic

The precise use of language is very important to me, but I can't get excited about "scam." Every natural language exists in tension between rules that define how the most powerful people of that tradition spoke one or two or five hundred years earlier, and popular usage, which is in constant flux. Most changes in popular usage are forgotten when the generation that invented them dies off. A few persist and become accepted usage. Then "the rules" must change to explain why they are natural and right.

True, the new uses of "scam" skip over defining exactly what is a scam: "[Today's atmosphere of alarm over the dangers of drinking] alcohol is a scam." English has always done that. "Jane drinks excessively." Drinks what... water, soda pop, Red Bull? Custom tells us that "drinks" without an object usually refers to alcohol.

So I consider the diatribe against "scam" a bit of column filler; sound and fury signifying nothing. In a generation this use of "scam" will probably be remembered, if at all, as quaint. Maybe, just maybe, it will become accepted usage, and people will wonder how it could ever have been different. In either case the world will survive, or not, regardless.

The Zeus investigators are to be congratulated for performing a major trial in patients for whom there is a major treatment gap. The negative outcome of Zeus far from the end of the anti-inflammatory theory but rather another important step in understanding the significant challenges of reducing cardiovascular risk in patients with renal failure and high cardiovascular risk as assessed by hsCRP (an excellent marker of prognosis). The results indicate the need to target a broader range of inflammatory pathways rather than a specific pathway, and also inform trialists that a reduction in hsCRP is not a surrogate marker for clinical efficacy.
This may be one reason why low-dose colchicine which is currently the only FDA approved anti-inflammatory drug showed its effects, and at low dose has been found to be safe and well tolerated.  It is not time to walking away from this investigational pathway but rather time to embrace it. 
(PI of LoDoCo2 trial)

There are tons of theories about heart disease and what causes it. But there are people who have very high LDL and other "issues" yet they do NOT have heart disease. For instance, the idea that EVERYONE with high LDL is doomed is false.

The recurring bottom line on heart disease is: You can't outrun your genetics.

And, however much scientists can't stand it, some people have genetics that make their high LDL a non-issue, etc.

Generations of cardiologists have not been able to figure out why some families that eat "the wrong food" (high fat, etc.), and have "bad" blood work, and are who are overweight are nevertheless able to live without evident heart disease into their 90's.

My mother had a 1st cousin whose overall health should have made her a sitting duck for dying of heart disease, but apparently her DNA didn't get the memo, b/c she lived to be a couple of months shy of her 100th birthday, and she still did not have heart disease! It confounded her doctors and they had a hard time "accepting" this woman who was a living refutation of all their "rules"!

comments.name: Deb Rivera

The issue is a loss of redox balance, with inflammation being an intended trigger. Prolonged and extreme redox deviation from homeostasis can trigger ferroptosis -- the type of cell death at the heart of cardiovascular disease and neurodegen. Dean Jone's work on Redox -- and Martin Feelish's work both speak to a very interesting framework that answers a lot of the mysteries we are all pondering, tho there work is mostly siloed in fringe journals. With GLP-1ra's coming to prominence I think it is time to fold in those fringe fields--not to mention the dysautonomia and increased metabolic disorders plaguing our society. At the very least can we include the fringe Anti-oxidant and redox journals when building AI knowledge bases? Just because the kinetics of the free-radical model didn't hold, it doesn't mean that all of redox needs to be largely left out of our models. I stand by redox metabolomics as the missing omics -- I mean, most of our key proteins actually change structure and function depending on their oxidation state -- including insulin.

comments.location: Michigan (the heart of the Great Lakes)
comments.body: I grew up in working class metro Detroit, a child of people whose economic fortunes were tied to manufacturing, especially the automobile industry. Tony Bourdain was born 10 days after I was. The era he grew up in was in many ways the era I grew up in. And when he made the leap from line cook to stardom, something that felt very accidental, he took me (& others) along for the ride. Because of that I was exposed to places, people and situations that my working class life of job, caregiving and responsibility never allowed for. I’m grateful for that. But along the way I also saw many of the challenges and struggles that his stardom didn’t disguise. Unlike so many who create a public persona disconnected from an inner reality Tony remained present with himself even when enlightening and entertaining others. I’m also grateful for that as well. And for sharing my passion for the work of Michigan born Jim Harrison, poet, novelist, screenplay writer and gourmand who appeared on two of Tony’s shows and who Tony treated with a childlike awe, which I certainly shared. That being said I don’t think that Anthony Bourdain would appreciate the level of cultishness that has grown up around his legacy. He struggled to reach a level of reality in his work that few in the industry had any interest in doing. His shows were never just about food or travel, only how those things led him to understanding and knowing the people behind them and that is his legacy, not all this marketing nonsense.

Articles like this, Ms. Callimachi--

--are fascinating.  Even to guys. 

Thank you. 

But I found myself remembering Alexander Pope's poem "The Rape of the Lock."  

Rape, you understand, meaning theft.  

And oh the details.  Lovingly, almost pruriently described.  As the beauteous Belinda (attended by a maid) seats herself at her vanity.  And looks into the mirror.  

             "A beauteous image in the glass appears.
              To that she bends, to that her eyes she rears.
              Th' inferior priestess at the altar's side
               Trembling begins the sacred rites of Pride."  

But oh the accoutrements, the paraphernalia required! 

                "This casket India's glowing gems unlocks
                  And all Arabia breathes from yonder box."    

On and on it goes.  Detail after marvelous detail.  I love it.  

Did I mention guys?  

Years ago, I was subbing in a high school.  And some of those boys! 

--they didn't make life easier for a poor sub.  Noisy, inattentive, undisciplined. I didn't much like them. 

BUT--

--between classes one day, I strayed into the men's room.  

And my goodness!

There they stood, those guys!  Staring intently at a mirror just inside the door.  It was old and dim.  You could hardly make out your reflection--

--but these guys were combing their hair.   It was as if they were performing surgery.  Not a hair out of place! 

And they call it a vanity.  

I wonder why.  

Thanks again, Ms. Callimachi.

Not having to contort oneself in front of the bathroom mirror is making a huge difference. I have a comfortable place (totally my space to apply (& practice)and room for it all. The morning and evening ritual is comforting and calming. I’ve rarely worn makeup throughout my life - just eyeshadow and mascara. Using an eyebrow color wand makes a huge difference in my face’s appearance now that the middle to outer hairs turned gray.  The makeup I’m learning to apply looks good now that I’m gaining some skills. I feel (and look) better. I do it mostly for me.

The skincare routine was something I should have started many decades ago. I’m really enjoying the ritual - and my aged skin is looking better. 

I’m so glad that I bought the vanity!

As resident of nearby Nelson, over the decades I have observed the influx of festival goers come into town to stock up on provisions for this annual festival. We also see them return afterwards trying to regain their equilibrium after a weekend of drug use and lack of sleep. 

In addition to this year’s 600 to 800 medical emergencies over the weekend cited in your article, attendees put others at risk by their driving behaviours. 

BC Highway Patrol maintained two roadblocks at the end of the festival, which resulted in the following:

311 tickets for speeding,

57 vehicles towed for mechanical safety or driver impairment,

51 24-hour driving suspensions for drug impairment,

85 Standardized Field Sobriety Tests for suspected drug-impaired driving,

30 Drug Recognition Expert evaluations resulting in 27 impaired-by-drug investigations and 23 blood draws by a lab technician,

50 violation tickets for a variety of BC MVA offences,

8 vehicles immediately removed from the road due to major mechanical defects.

Hundreds of violation tickets including 11 for no insurance. 

“We asked people before the event to make sure they allowed drugs to clear their system before driving, but too many ignored that advice,” Sgt. McLaughlin said. “It looks like we will have to be back next year, and hopefully in greater numbers, to deal with festival-goers who are driving unsafely.”

Japan’s urban population grew from roughly 59 million in 1960 to a peak of about 115 million in the 2010s, and now sits at approx. 113.9 million. The proportion living in cities has reached an all-time high of over 92%.
Post-War Industrial Boom (1950–1979)
***1950: Urban areas comprise roughly 37% of the total national population.
***1960: World Bank data notes urban population is 63% of the total. 
Modern Urbanization and Peak (1980–2010)
***1990: Greater Tokyo continues upward, absorbing over 30% of total demographic footprint.
***2010: Census reports 90.7% of population lives in urban areas
Recent Decline (2011–Present)
***2011–2020: Population contraction; urban percentage climbs as rural towns shrink.
***2022–2026: The percentage of urban dwellers: ~92.1%.
---------------

Hosts receive labor and a bit of cultural exchange while avoiding long term residence that might fuel concerns for cultural dilution. Farmers in my PNW region use this organization to run their small operations with pretty fair results!  
Second, there are dozens of former federal employees available who have extensive experience working with hazard and nuisance animals (including habituated bears), who would probably be delighted by the opportunity to work in Japan adjusting the behaviors of these animals.  These people are friendly, well trained and professional, and are likely currently underutilized.  Could be an effective and mutually beneficial solution!  
Best regards and thanks for a great article.

Someone loses a case as between the employee and the union, or as between an employer and a union, and the loser appeals like any court decision can be appealed.  That fact hearing is over and the appeal goes up on the established record.  

If you're saying the original fact hearing did not afford due process, that's one thing and certainly is a legitimate position, I've had the same issue on that for years.  And if you're saying that the investigative and hearing processes should not be within the same agency, I certainly agree with that, they all work in the same offices and are buddies.  And do these agencies function as advocates?  Yes, they certainly do, and in the labor context it is usually in favor of the union whether the other party was a member or an employer.  

So I'm kind of confused on what your point is?  If agencies, labor or otherwise, can't defend a hearing officer's or ALJ's decision, then are you saying they don't get to particpate in appeals of their own decisions and the state agency should defer to  winning party to defend the agency? comments.body: Steven Foukal, the "digital wellness entrepreneur" quoted here, left Thailand for Vietnam because, in his words, "more and more people want an escape." That sentence is the whole psychology of this migration: a country with a war, a French occupation, and a legal system built partly to punish the vices colonizers once used to pacify it, treated as a cheaper backdrop for content once Bangkok tightened its visa rules. A Da Nang resident says his quiet block got rezoned for nightlife four years ago, and he now opens his door most mornings to drunks asleep on the pavement. Nobody arriving is reading up on Vietnamese history, they're doing visa arbitrage: Cambodia cracked down on scam compounds, Thailand shortened its visa window, so both the nomads and the fraud rings moved next door. A man rips his shirt off and chokes a stranger, and the coverage pivots to how harsh Vietnam's courts are rather than to why a country this affordable keeps absorbing people this entitled. Many had completed university education in hospitality and were worried they would have to find work abroad.

It was, at that time, fairly uncrowded and it wasn't difficult to do pretty much anything you wanted. I definitely enjoyed it more than Thailand and while I would later discover that traveling into the highlands is the right way to visit Thailand, back then you were still mostly encouraged not to go north of Bangkok.

Western attitudes towards criminality don't work even for the non-communist East and Southeast Asian states. We tend to view criminal behavior as a personal failing, while in those cultures it is typically viewed as a familial failing. When the state is forced to intervene, its intent is to send a message to the entire family to handle their own business going forward.

Here's a take on Puerto Rican politics that seems not to have made it in the letters advocating statehood or independence.

Good luck!

I first came to Hood River County in 1986, drawn by its amazing mix of agriculture and recreation opportunities. After spending 20 summers here-meeting my wife here- we decided, when we found out she was pregnant, that this was the place we wanted to raise our family. In all of my time here we have dealt with wildfire smoke but the drought this winter had everyone on edge. Now it’s real. 

Yesterday I went out to pick blueberries in my front yard and had to put on my N95 that has sat in a drawer for 6 years. I have a constant headache. Air filters are cranking all day and night. 

Yes, these are all first world problems and the result of fire suppression, the constant drive for more building, more everything, all in combination with climate change. But somehow this feels more precarious having started my morning reading about energy sucking data centers and the incompetence of Doug Burgum and other deniers that go right to the top. It's been 18 days since I started noting that I couldn't go out for a hike or walk or bike ride due to smoke. Oh, and did I mention that the high today is 104? Yup, I'm whining. I know I'm lucky I have an HVAC system and air filters running full time. I'm good as long as I stay indoors. But as others have noted, it's the mental aspect that has become the problem. I empathize with others going through the same experience—or worse. I mean, think of the ranchers, the farmers whose livelihood has been all but erased.  Learn to live with it? comments.body: I live in Seattle with my family and have lived here since 2008. I spend a lot of time in the North Cascades east of Seattle and have seen the changes in the environment over the years. Each year it gets a little hotter and dryer. The rains usually start in October and last until the end of May. Around November it gets cold enough that the rains turn into snow and build the snowpack for the summer. Not this year. It didn’t get cold enough in the mountains so all that rain rushed down the mountains and created some of the worst flooding on record. The ski resorts suffered. They could barely keep them open. I knew that the 2026 summer would be horrible. We still have about 3 months to go before the rains come again. Global warming is real.

comments.name: Dog

Over 2 million acres have burned in Oregon so far this year. That’s an area about the size of Puerto Rico. This year’s fire total already breaks the record set over the entire 2024 fire season. It’s early August. Fire season lasts until October. Eastern Oregon is burning and Western Oregon is a tinderbox just waiting for the right conditions. 

I’m in Portland. I have asthma. I’m running two HEPA air filters full blast in my apartment. It sounds like an airport jetway. For the last two days I could feel ashes in my mouth even with the filters running. Lots of hits on the rescue inhaler, and I’m alternating between an N95 and a P100 respirator when I have to go outside (and sometimes inside, too). Hard to sleep through the night. It’s exhausting. 

I need to leave here for my health but I am stuck in my job until I retire, assuming there’s anything left to retire from by then. I’m worried the safe places will be overrun by the wealthy by the time I can go. 

I feel guilty complaining about my first-world problems. I can’t help but worry about the homeless folks in my neighborhood. Many of them are in very poor health and many of them won’t accept help. 

The smoke is dissipating for now and the particulates are starting to clear here. We still have an ozone alert until tomorrow evening, assuming they don’t extend it again. 

People are tired and stressed. There is also a band down the street playing music outside.  

But I have cute cats, so there’s that, I guess.

comments.body:
There's a lot of talk about robots replacing us, i.e., as a species, which is purely science fiction. 

One of the things about robots is that they are extremely high-maintenance devices, and require highly-skilled people with a panoply of skills to design, build and repair them. Just think of the organisational nous necessary to run the business, to project-manage the design, the supply chain coordination to purchase the parts and materials necessary to manufacture the robots, the complex machinery to assemble them, and when one fails (in hardware and/or software) the ability to diagnose and fix the problem, to disassemble, replace parts, reassemble. Even in science fiction movies it's still humans doing all that work. We can always just keep them away from electrical outlets, not charge their batteries.

It might also be noted that "autonomy" is an important word here: much of the hype, such as the recent dancing robots video from China, even those marketing videos from Boston Dynamics, are either preprogrammed routines or remote-controlled by humans, they're not demonstrations of creative, autonomous choreography any more than are night-time drone "fireworks" displays, i.e., impressive in their own right, but hardly anything to worry about as some kind of nascent, silicon-based species.

A lot of AI and robotics marketing is about fear. Fear has always been very effective at selling product.

We went down to the river and saw Lions, elephants and many other animals. For Tanzania, I highly recommend a local agent. If you go to TripAdvisor, you will see a list of recommended operators. If you want a  private Safari you will save money by going with a local operator. I can highly recommend Basecamp Tanzania which we used for our first Safari, and Bright African safaris who we used for our second. Our second was in late February early March where the migration was in Indutu just south of Serengeti. We saw millions of animals there. It was a little bit late for the calving that year but we saw many, many young wildebeest and cheetahs and lions on the hunt. We are heading out in a few days for another adventure this time. comments.body:
As a former international teacher based for 5 years in Abuja, I traveled during school breaks to Cape Town, Nairobi, and other classic safari destinations.

If a safari is your main goal, this article's advice is fine.  

I'd suggest there's much more to see across Africa, and keep in mind you're most likely visiting 1 or maybe 2 or 3 of the continent's 50 odd nations: there's much you'll end up missing no matter what.  

I like Cape Town and Stellenbosch, one of the nearby wine regions with its own beauty, hiking, and nearby beaches.  It's a fine introduction to Africa, but the recent unrest against immigrants would make me hesitate.  

Kenya is well worth exploring too, although I found it more effective to skip the overpriced tourist sites, and work with a local to see more hidden spots, like caves and former guerilla camps from the Mau-Mau uprising that preceded independence there.  

Nigeria's security makes travel within the nation difficult, but Yankari, West Africa's oldest wildlife preserve, is worth the effort.  It's a day's drive from the capital, in Bauchi state.  Nok village is closer, in Kaduna, as are other cultural attractions.  

My advice would be to research ahead of time and then chose a destination, making the safari part of a more extensive exploration of your chosen destination.  

Consider avoiding the best known spots: Uganda instead of Rwanda for gorillas.  It'll save a lot.  

See the people, talk to them.  Learn from them.  Then decide what to do.

Burberry like? I love Burberry but you’re hundreds of years off in your style assessment. That so Canadian it could be our flag print has existed longer than the country. A more primitive version was used by fur trappers and voyagers in our early history. The version most often (and still) worn throughput Canada was first refined as a part of the uniform of the early forestry business and remains important because in a country where forest are ancient, dense and used by Canadians for hiking, leisure, industry and hunting that red plaid is a warm safety vest ensuring forestry workers are visible.

In many parts of rural Canadian (Northern Ontario, Maritimes & BC interior to name a few) it’s jokingly referred to as the Canadian dinner jacket. Every Canadian young adult or teenager at some point in their lives had one as they continue to have eras as fashion requirements along with other uniquely Canadian clothing items. In my teens having one and either a pair of Mukluks or Kodiak boots (laces loose of course) was non negotiable. Then there was Bob & Doug McKenzie fictitious brothers created by Rick Moranis & Dave Thomas on SCTV whose uniform was the Canadian dinner jacket. Their segments became so wildly popular they did cross overs on Saturday Night Live, had a best selling comedy album with the hit single Take Off featuring Geddy Lee the very Canadian lead singer of the legendary Canadian rock band Rush. comments.name: culturejamming-M LeVine
comments.body:
Wow! An entire article on country music in Africa, and not a single mention that country music is in good measure from Africa. The banjo is an African instrument. Versions of the violin and the guitar have existed in Africa for thousands of year. The origins of country music in the US lie in the deep south, with the field hollers and songs of the African slaves and their descendants, which then mixed together with Irish, cajun and Indigenous musics to create the genre we all know. Even the country twang has direct African roots. Indeed, it wasn't called "country" till it was raced in the 1920s and black and white artists were separated. 

But for Africans who started hearing country music almost as soon as the first records hit the Continent not long after the genre emerged, it just sounded like home. And yes, Africans have lots of "cowboys" and they don't just were stetsons. Polo is very big in Nigeria, Kenya and across Africa as well.

As a former historian of Japan (now retired) who taught courses on the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, I first believed as a historical fact that those bombings led directly to the end of the war. And I taught it that way for years.

However, every time I taught that course I dug deeper into the primary sources regarding the Japanese surrender, and could find no evidence that the atomic bombings were the primary concern of the Japanese high command. Rather, they saw them in the context of, for example, the incendiary bombing of Tokyo on the night of March 9-10, 1945, which also killed approximately 140,000 persons.

Any explanation of the Japanese surrender requires the inclusion of the Soviet declaration of war on Japan. The Soviets wanted badly to split Japan just as Germany had been split. The Japanese wanted to keep their country whole and knew that the Americans were as anti-Communist as they were. It was an advantage to the Japanese to surrender to the Americans, which they did on August 15, 1945. Nevertheless, the Soviets did not agree to a cease-fire until August 22.

According to Veteran Tributes, Lieutenant Beser was the only crewmember who flew on both atomic bombing missions, which led virtually immediately to Japan’s surrender.  His name appears as one of three specialists listed on Capt. Lewis’ notepad. No matter what our opinions are about the worthiness of atomic energy as a legitimate military tool, we’ve got to reckon the weight of the actions of these crew members and hopefully the gravitas they carried with them forever after.

Of course, today is the anniversary of Hiroshima. Reading these articles got me thinking about nuclear weapons and especially the risks they present to the survival of all life on Earth, and Earth itself. We Americans need to place this issue front and center in our politics as the United States now promotes nuclear proliferation in the Middle East even as it professes to limit it.

Joseph Appel
Woodstock, NY

I first became aware of capybaras as a kid, when I read Bill Peet’s delightful 1966 book, “Capyboppy”. Peet was for many years a Disney animator, joining the studio in the late 1930s to work on “Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs”, and remaining there till the early 1960s. He focused on writing and illustrating children’s books after leaving animation.

“Capyboppy” is based on his family’s adoption of a young capybara (in an era when trade in exotic pets was less regulated than it is now); the title is the name they gave their new pet. It was generally an amiable addition to the family, but they ultimately had to keep it outside at night, since, like all rodents, it chewed constantly, and the huge critter would destroy their furniture if left unsupervised.

This exclusion from the family, however, distressed the capybara, a highly social animal. Capyboppy became moody and erratic. Eventually, they reluctantly decided that it was not safe to keep the big and sometimes irritable animal in their household, and they donated it to a local zoo (that already had other capybaras), where they could visit Capyboppy regularly.

The Gulf Arab states like Saudi Arabia have realized that the U.S. cannot provide real security, that Israel comes first at their own detriment, and that the security architecture needs to be completely rethought. The ultimate reconciliation will occur--and it will happen, it's a matter of time--between Iran and Saudi Arabia, meaning the Shia and Sunni worlds, as America's exit from the Middle East becomes more and more of a reality. The skirmishes on the edges we're seeing now, with proxies being funded by either side of the Shia-Sunni divide, are only a historical footnote. The Islamic world's coming reunification under something resembling the revitalized ummah is part of the world's center of gravity moving toward Asia. By the middle of the century the world's greatest energies will be in the Sino-Islamic corridor, with countries on the periphery in Europe, Australasia, and Africa joining the grand alliance. This new security alliance is very tentative but it is a move in the right direction, after fifty years of the U.S. successfully thwarting unification by stepping up its role in the Middle East starting in the early 1970s. comments.name: N.G. Krishnan

​This strategic agreement feels straight out of Aesop’s fable of The Frog and the Mouse—where two uneasy allies tie themselves together for mutual protection, only to find that tethering disparate, vulnerable bodies together in turbulent waters usually ends up dragging everyone down under the eyes of the hawk.

​The sheer tragedy of this treaty lies in its desperation. You have a cash-flush Gulf monarchy looking for hard power and potential nuclear insurance, a nuclear-armed state plagued by chronic economic collapse, and a NATO member balancing its own regional ambitions—all trying to construct a cohesive defense shield out of fundamentally conflicting priorities.

​When you treat an attack on one as an attack on all in a region overflowing with volatile rivalries, a minor flare-up on one front risks dragging all three into a catastrophic spiral nobody actually wants. 

It’s a classic geopolitical tragedy: an alliance born to manufacture stability through collective deterrence, but so structurally fragile that it might instead guarantee shared ruin.

Really enjoyed the movie. A solid 4 out of 5, despite having vaguely Star Trek V vibes. 

The problem with Korra was, for the first two seasons, she didn't want to be a hero. Neither did Aang, that's how he ended up in the ball of ice, but that was his backstory, not the focus. Once she accepted the journey, as it were, the show took off. And I really liked the steampunk setting, whose rise isn't so far-fetched in the new world of metal bending. 

As for the live action show, it's ok. The first season was disappointing only because the memory of arguably the greatest animated show ever got in the way. The second season is more confident in letting it be what it is. Special points for how they reworked and improved Iroh's story from "Tales of Ba Sing Se," one of the two best original episodes.

comments.name: Thomas Radke
comments.body: A personal note to Mr. Barker. I too was involved in an airplane incident which I survived (obviously) and after which I vowed never to fly again. I was flying back from a business trip from Peoria, Illinois with 9 coworkers and 2 pilots in an old twin engine Cessena. Over the border of Iowa and Minnesota we ran into a very bad storm front which threw our plane down towards the ground. We turned sideways and nose down. Everything not tied down inside the interior began to free float like in space. I actually ripped the arm rest completely off my seat. We all assumed that we were dead meat. Suddenly the engines were growling like an old Sky King TV show and we leveled out but as we we flying level just above the ground we were not out of trouble. Trees separating corn fields lay ahead and the pilots barely cleared them. We could hear the bottom of the plane hitting the top branches.  I turned in my seat and screamed at the pilots "what did you do"?; he replied that he'd thrown out the landing gear to find a way to level the plane. Smart thinking. When we landed I reached beneath the plane and pulled a long corn stalk out of a wheel assembly. We we literally that close to crashing. I couldn't keep my vow to never fly again as 2 weeks later we were all again on that same plane heading to Peoria. Besides, I wanted to fly back to Germany and that's a long boat ride. Don't give up on flying. It's very safe compared to other ways of traveling. If your time is up then it's up.
